title.zh: 写到一半才想起的两条
title.en: Two Clauses He Thought of Midway Through Writing

dek.zh: 阿波马托克斯的受降条件里，军官的佩刀和私马私物都不是谈出来的——是格兰特写条文时自行加进去的；士兵的马骡则是李问起后，格兰特口头准许的，没有写进条文。
dek.en: At Appomattox, the officers' side-arms and their private horses and effects were never negotiated: Grant wrote them into the terms on his own, partway through the draft. The soldiers' own horses and mules came up only when Lee asked, and Grant allowed them verbally, without writing them into the terms.

heading.en: A Sick Headache, Mustard, and a Letter

paras.zh: 8日，格兰特跟着在李军后方的波托马克军行进，正犯着重头痛，在路边一处离大部队有一段距离的农舍过夜，把脚泡进热水和芥末，手腕和后颈贴上芥末膏，指望天亮就能好。李来信提议会面。格兰特的回信很干脆：他无权谈和，这样的会面不可能有好结果；和平的条件众所周知，南方只要放下武器，就能让和平早点到来，救下成千上万条人命和数以亿计尚未被毁的财产。
paras.en: On the 8th Grant followed the Army of the Potomac, which was in rear of Lee, in the grip of a sick headache. He spent the night at a farmhouse on the road, some distance behind the main body of the army, bathing his feet in hot water and mustard and putting mustard plasters on his wrists and the back of his neck, hoping that by morning he would be cured. A letter from Lee proposed a meeting. Grant's answer was brisk. He had no authority to treat on the subject of peace, and the proposed meeting could lead to no good. The terms on which peace could be had, he wrote, were well understood: let the South lay down its arms, and the most desirable event would come sooner, sparing thousands of lives and hundreds of millions of property not yet destroyed.

paras.zh: 难处在于，受降条件得由他自己定。眼下没有草案，没有你来我往的条款拉锯，对方要的是他开出的条件。格兰特最后写下的那份条款里，有两处是落笔之后才想起来加进去的：军官的佩刀，以及军官的私马和私物。南军士兵自己的马骡则根本不在条文里，是李问起后格兰特口头准许的。
paras.en: The difficulty was that the terms of surrender were his to write. There was no draft on the table, no haggling over clauses back and forth — the other side was simply asking him to name his conditions. Two items in the terms he finally set down were afterthoughts, added only once his pen was already moving: the officers' side-arms, and the officers' private horses and effects. The horses and mules belonging to the Confederate enlisted men were not in the written terms at all; Grant allowed them verbally, after Lee asked.

heading.zh: 停火疑虑与穿过战线的信
heading.en: Doubts About Halting the Fighting, and a Letter Sent Through the Lines

paras.zh: 格兰特回信说，他没有谈和的权限，南方放下武器就能让和平早日到来。此后李再次来信，可这封信送得很费劲：由于格兰特所走的路线，这封信很可能无法在约定时间内送到他手里并带回答复，除非信使穿过南军战线。因此，李派人护送带信的军官穿过自己的战线，把信送到格兰特手里。另据格兰特记述，米德和谢里登都对是否停火非常犹豫，怕这不是真心求和；而且北弗吉尼亚军团已无路可逃，除非用诡计脱身。
paras.en: Grant replied that he had no authority to treat on the subject of peace, and that by laying down their arms the South would hasten peace. Lee then wrote again, but this message was hard to deliver: from the route Grant had taken, it would probably not be possible to reach him and get an answer back within the time fixed unless the messenger passed through the rebel lines. Lee therefore sent an escort with the officer bearing the message through his own lines to Grant. Separately, Grant records that Meade and Sheridan both hesitated very considerably about suspending hostilities at all. They were afraid the overture was not in good faith; and the Army of Northern Virginia was where it could not escape except by some deception.

paras.zh: 格兰特收到信时还在头痛，一看到信的内容就好了。他回信说，因为他已从里士满—林奇堡路转到法姆维尔—林奇堡路，上午11点50分才拿到信；此刻在沃克教堂以西约四英里，正向前赶去会面，请对方在这条路上通知会面地点。赶到谢里登那里时，那里的人情绪激动，表示认为这是南军脱身的诡计：他们相信约翰斯顿正从北卡罗来纳北上，李要去会合；只要格兰特点头，五分钟内就能把对方打垮。格兰特不怀疑李的诚意，不久便被领到李所在之处。
paras.en: The officer found Grant still suffering with the sick headache; in Grant's own telling, "the instant I saw the contents of the note I was cured." He wrote back at once. Lee's note had reached him only at 11:50 a.m., he explained, because he had passed from the Richmond and Lynchburg road to the Farmville and Lynchburg road; he was at that moment about four miles west of Walker's Church and would push forward to the front for the meeting; a message left on this road naming the place would reach him. When he rode up to Sheridan's position, the men there were very much excited. They expressed their view that the whole thing was a ruse to let the Confederates get away. Johnston, they believed, was marching up from North Carolina and Lee moving to join him, and they would whip the rebels where they stood in five minutes if only Grant would let them go in. Grant had no doubt of Lee's good faith, and was soon conducted to where he was.

heading.en: The Meeting at the McLean House

paras.zh: 会面在阿波马托克斯考特豪斯一位麦克莱恩先生的房子里，李带着参谋马歇尔上校等在那里。格兰特当天一早离营时没料到结果来得这么快，因此穿着很随便：士兵短上衣，肩上钉着军衔肩章以示身份；也没带佩剑，他骑马在战场上时通常就不带。
paras.en: The meeting took place at the house of a Mr. McLean at Appomattox Court House, where Lee waited with Colonel Marshall, one of his staff officers. Grant had left camp that morning with no inkling that the end would come so quickly, and so he was in rough garb: a soldier's blouse for a coat, with the shoulder straps of his rank so the army would know who he was, and no sword, as he usually went without one when riding the field.

paras.zh: 格兰特写明，他不知道李是什么心情。按他的描述，李神情庄重、喜怒不形于色，看不出是为战争终于结束而高兴，还是为结局难过而不肯表露。倒是他自己，收到信时满心欢喜，此刻却变得低落。
paras.en: Grant was explicit that he did not know what Lee was feeling. In Grant's description, Lee was a man of much dignity with an impassible face; it was impossible to say whether he was inwardly glad the end had finally come, or sad at the result and too manly to show it. Whatever his feelings, they were entirely concealed from Grant's observation. Grant's own were a different matter: jubilant on receipt of the letter, he now found them sad and depressed.

paras.zh: 两人先闲谈，谈得很愉快，格兰特几乎忘了此行的目的。过了一阵，李把话题拉回来，说他此来就是想拿到格兰特准备给他军队的条件。格兰特说，他的意思只是让军队放下武器，战争期间未经正式交换不得再拿起武器。李说，他读信时就是这样理解的。
paras.en: The two men first talked, so pleasantly that Grant almost forgot the object of their meeting. After a while Lee brought the conversation back to it: he had asked for this interview, he said, to get from Grant the terms he proposed to give his army. Grant answered that he meant merely that the army should lay down their arms, not to take them up again during the continuance of the war unless duly and properly exchanged. Lee said he had so understood the letter.

paras.zh: 又谈了几句，李再次打断话头，建议把条件写成文字。格兰特叫他幕中担任秘书的帕克将军取来纸笔，开始写。他后来说，落笔时连第一个词该写什么都不知道，只想着把自己心里的意思表达清楚，让人不会误会；写到一半，想起军官的私马和私物对他们很重要，对己方却毫无用处，而要他们交出佩刀是不必要的羞辱。
paras.en: They talked on a little longer, and then Lee interrupted again to suggest that the terms ought to be written out. Grant called to General Parker, secretary on his staff, for writing materials and began to write. As he later told it, when he put pen to paper he did not know the first word he should use. He knew only what was in his mind and wanted to express it clearly, so there could be no mistaking it. As he wrote on, it occurred to him that the officers had private horses and effects that were important to them and of no value to the Union, and that "it would be an unnecessary humiliation to call upon them to deliver their side arms."

paras.zh: 写成的条款是这样：官兵名册一式两份，一份交格兰特指定的军官，一份由李指定的人留存；军官个人宣誓，连队或团级长官为所部具结，未经正式交换不再对美国政府作战；武器、火炮和公物停车列队、堆放上交；但军官的佩刀、私人物品和私马不在此列；事情办完，官兵各自回乡，只要遵守宣誓和所居地的法律，不受联邦当局打扰。
paras.en: What he wrote ran roughly as follows. Rolls of all the officers and men were to be made in duplicate, one copy given to an officer designated by Grant, the other retained by whoever Lee designated. Officers would give individual paroles not to take up arms against the United States until properly exchanged, and each company or regimental commander would sign a like parole for the men of his command. The arms, artillery and public property were to be parked and stacked and turned over to the officer appointed to receive them — but this did not embrace the officers' side-arms, nor their private horses or baggage. That done, each officer and man would be allowed to return home, not to be disturbed by United States authority so long as he observed his parole and the laws in force where he resided.

paras.zh: 此前两人没有一个字谈到私产、佩刀或类似问题。李看来对最初提出的条件并无异议；或者即便有意见，也想等条件写成文字再提。李读到佩刀、马匹和军官私物这一段时，说这会对他的军队有良好影响；格兰特说他讲这话时带着感情，并注明那只是自己当时的看法。至于流传甚广的李献剑、格兰特再把剑退回，格兰特把这件事以及关于它的许多其他说法直斥为“纯属虚构的传奇”：直到他把这一句写进条文，两人都没提过剑或佩刀，这不是预谋，是写到那里才想起来的。他还说，假如自己碰巧漏写、而李提了出来，他也会把这一项照样写进条款，就像他同意让士兵留下马匹那一条一样。
paras.en: Not one word had passed between the two men about private property, side-arms or anything of the kind. Lee appeared to have no objection to the terms first proposed, or if he had a point against them he preferred to wait until they were in writing. When he read the passage about side-arms, horses and the officers' private property, he remarked with some feeling, Grant thought, that this would have a happy effect upon his army. As for the famous story of Lee surrendering his sword and Grant handing it back, Grant dismissed it and much else said about the occasion as "the purest romance." Until he wrote it into the terms, neither man had mentioned sword or side-arms. There was no premeditation: the thought did not occur to him until the moment he set it down. Had he happened to omit it and Lee called his attention to it, he said, he would have put it in precisely as he acceded to the provision about the soldiers keeping their horses.

paras.zh: 接着李又说，他们的军队编制和联邦军不太一样（格兰特注意到，这话仍暗指双方是两个国家），骑兵和炮兵的马是自备的，问这些人能不能把马带走。格兰特回答，按写好的条文不行，只有军官可以带走私物。说完他接着讲了一段：他估计这大概是这场战争的最后一仗，他真心希望如此；据他看来，士兵多半是小农，地方已被两军搜掠殆尽，没有手边的马，恐怕种不出养活一家人过冬的收成。美国不需要这些牲口，所以他要交代留守受降的军官：凡自称有马或骡的南军士兵，都可以把牲口牵回家。
paras.en: Then Lee remarked that their army was organized a little differently from that of the United States — still implying, Grant noted, that they were two countries — and that in their army the cavalrymen and artillerists owned their own horses. Was he to understand that the men who owned their horses could keep them? As the terms stood, Grant said, they could not; only the officers were permitted to take their private property. He then went on. He thought this would be about the last battle of the war, and sincerely hoped so. He took it that most of the men in the ranks were small farmers, and the whole country had been so raided by the two armies that it was doubtful whether they could put in a crop to carry themselves and their families through the next winter without the horses they were riding. The United States did not want the animals, and he would therefore instruct the officers he left behind, while taking the paroles of Lee's troops, to let every man of the Confederate army who claimed to own a horse or mule take the animal home.

paras.zh: 李写信接受条件，说条款与格兰特8日来信中所提的实质相同，他将指定军官来办交接。在告辞之前，他说自己的军队状况很糟：缺粮，没有草料，士兵连日只吃炒玉米，需要请格兰特供应口粮和草料。格兰特说当然可以，问需要多少人的口粮，李答约两万五千人；格兰特便让李派自己的军需官和军需主任到两三英里外的阿波马托克斯车站，从被截停的列车上取用所需。
paras.en: Lee wrote accepting the terms: being substantially the same as those expressed in Grant's letter of the 8th, they were accepted, and he would designate the proper officers to carry the stipulations into effect. Before taking his leave he added that his army was in a very bad condition for want of food, and without forage; his men had been living for days on parched corn exclusively, and he would have to ask Grant for rations and forage. Grant agreed at once and asked how many men needed rations; about twenty-five thousand, Lee answered. Grant authorized him to send his own commissary and quartermaster to Appomattox Station, two or three miles away, where out of the trains the Union had stopped they could have all the provisions wanted.

paras.zh: 受降消息传到北军阵线，士兵们开始鸣放百响礼炮庆贺，格兰特立刻派人叫停：南军现在是俘虏，不该为他们的垮台而欢呼。第二天两人交谈时，李说，南方是个大国，也许要来回走三四遍，战事才能完全结束，不过对方已无力抵抗，做得到；他诚挚希望北军不必再被迫造成更多死伤和牺牲，但无法预言结果。格兰特请李出面劝全部南军投降，说以李的影响，必会被欣然接受；李说，不先征询总统，他不能那样做。
paras.en: When news of the surrender reached the Union lines, the men began firing a salute of a hundred guns in honor of the victory. Grant at once sent word to have it stopped: "The Confederates were now our prisoners, and we did not want to exult over their downfall." The next day, in the course of a conversation between the two men, Lee said the South was a big country, and Union troops might have to march over it three or four times before the war entirely ended — though it could now be done, since the South could no longer resist. He earnestly hoped, however, that the Union would not be called upon to cause more loss and sacrifice of life; he could not foretell the result. Grant then suggested that no man in the Confederacy had such influence with the soldiery and the whole people as Lee, and that if he would now advise the surrender of all the armies, his advice would be followed with alacrity. Lee said he could not do that without consulting the President first.

heading.en: The One Item Never Written Into the Terms

paras.zh: 一种解释是，佩刀和私马这两条的意义不在让步大小，而在它们出现的位置：不是谈判桌上换来的，是起草人自己写进去的。作者推断，写进条文的成本几乎为零——武器、火炮和公物反正都要上交；收益则是让名册、宣誓这些真正要执行的条款少遇阻力。对方读到这一段时的反应，据格兰特说，是这会对他的军队有良好影响。
paras.en: One reading of the side-arms and private horses is that what matters is not the size of the concession but where it appears: it was not traded for at the negotiating table but written in by the drafter himself. The inference here is that the cost was close to nil — arms, artillery and public property had to be surrendered anyway — while the payoff was less resistance to the clauses that actually had to be carried out, the rolls and the paroles. When Lee read that passage, Grant recorded, he remarked that this would have a happy effect upon his army.

paras.zh: 马骡那一项更实际。格兰特当场给出的理由是过冬的收成：收缴来的牲口对联邦没用，对回家的小农是活下去的工具。一种解释是，这一项针对的不是面子，而是协议签完之后能不能真的收场——人要回乡、要吃饭、要种地，前面那些条款才有执行的人。要提醒的是，这一项不在已写成的条文里，是格兰特当面答应李、将指示留守军官办理的。
paras.en: The horses and mules were the more practical item. The reason Grant gave on the spot was the winter crop: animals taken in surrender were of no use to the Union, but to small farmers going home they were the tools of survival. One reading is that this item addressed not face but whether the settlement could actually be wound up afterward — the men had to go home, eat, and plant, and only then were there people to carry out everything already written down. A caution: this was not in the terms as written; Grant told Lee he would instruct the officers left behind.

paras.zh: 至于叫停鸣炮，一种解释是，受降条件里最后一项从不写在纸上：胜利方当天说的第一句话。作者提出的替代做法是，把收缴佩刀之类的要求当作威慑保留下来，让对方记住谁说了算；代价可能是执行阶段对方不愿配合，因为真正要办的事——交名册、办宣誓、放人回乡——都得靠对方的人去做。
paras.en: As for halting the salute, one reading is that the last clause of any surrender is never set on paper: it is the first thing the winning side says that day. The alternative the writer offers is to keep demands such as handing over side-arms on the books as a reminder of who is in charge. The cost might be an unwillingness to cooperate in the carrying out, because the things that genuinely have to be done — delivering the rolls, taking the paroles, sending the men home — depend on the other side's people doing them.

paras.zh: 你是一家制造公司的运营负责人，正在和合作八年的物流供应商提前终止合同，终止条款由你起草。清单里列着归还制服、撕下车厢贴纸、交回印着公司标志的工牌，逐项拍照验收。先问一句：这些东西收回来对你有什么用？如果答案是几乎没用，那它更像佩刀，而不像公物；真正该写清楚的，是最后一车货的交接清单、未结费用的算法，和双方车辆改喷漆的过渡期。
paras.en: You run operations at a manufacturing company and are ending a contract early with a logistics provider you have worked with for eight years. You draft the termination terms. On the list: return the uniforms, scrape the decals off the trailers, hand in the badges with the company logo, photograph each item for sign-off. Ask one question first: what use are these things to you? If the honest answer is almost none, they are closer to side-arms than to public property. What deserves to be spelled out instead is the handover checklist for the last truckload, the formula for unsettled charges, and a transition window for repainting the vehicles on both sides.

paras.zh: 另一个场景：一次团队合并，旧系统的权限当然要收，交接文档当然要列。但旧的职级称呼、内部头衔、历年合影里的署名，要不要一并清理？同样的问题也落在公告里：合并达成那天，你在全员邮件第一段写的是庆祝胜利，还是把对方接下来的去处和交接时间表交代清楚。
paras.en: Another scenario: two teams merge. Access to the old systems obviously has to be revoked, and the handover documents obviously have to be listed. But what about the old grade titles, the internal honorifics, the names printed on years of staff photos — should those be scrubbed as well? The same question lands on the announcement: on the day the merger closes, does the first paragraph of your all-staff email celebrate the win, or lay out where the other side goes next and the handover schedule?

paras.zh: 本文唯一的史源是格兰特本人的回忆录，标注年份为1885–86年，成书于事件之后。文中对话都是他的转述，未必逐字；米德、谢里登、李的说法也都经他一手记录。
paras.en: The sole source for this article is Grant's own memoirs, dated 1885–86 and written after the events. Every conversation in them is his retelling and need not be verbatim, and the words of Meade, Sheridan and Lee all reach us through him alone.

paras.zh: 他明确说自己不知道李的心情；说李带着感情讲话时，也注明那只是他当时的猜测。两边的心理都不该替他们补上。
paras.en: He states plainly that he did not know Lee's feelings, and where he says Lee spoke with feeling he flags it as his own guess at the time. Neither man's inner state should be filled in on his behalf.

paras.zh: 马骡的宽许不在已写成的条文里，是格兰特当面对李承诺、将指示留守军官办理的；落实得如何，原文没有交代；名册、宣誓这些条件怎样逐项执行，同样没有记载。日期只按原文「the 8th」这样的写法转述，不补出原文没有的年份。
paras.en: The indulgence on horses and mules was not in the terms as written; Grant promised Lee he would instruct the officers left behind to allow it. How far it was carried out the source does not say, and neither does it record how the rolls and paroles were executed item by item. Dates are kept as the source has them — "the 8th" and the like — with no year added that the original does not give.

scenario.zh: 你要和一位合作多年、日后仍在这个行业里做事的顾问谈结束合作的条款，草案由你来写。
scenario.en: You are negotiating the terms for ending a long-running engagement with a consultant you have worked with for years, someone who will go on working in the same industry, and you are the one drafting the terms.

question.zh: 这份条款里，哪些要求删掉反而让协议更好执行？哪些宽许该写进纸面，哪些可以口头交代并指定落实人？达成那天，你说的第一句话是什么？
question.en: Which requirements in the draft would make the agreement easier to carry out if they were deleted? Which indulgences belong on paper, and which can be left verbal with a named person responsible for seeing them through? And on the day it is settled, what is the first thing you say?

assumptions.zh:
对方日后仍可能与你或你的同行合作
交接、保密、结款这些真正要执行的条款需要对方人员配合
你方内部有人希望在条款里看到大获全胜的姿态
assumptions.en:
The other side may well work with you, or with your competitors, again
The clauses that actually have to be executed — handover, confidentiality, final settlement — need their people to cooperate
Some on your side want to see a posture of total victory in the terms

steps.zh:
把全部要求分成三类：必须收回的、对己方无用而对对方是羞辱的、影响对方生计的
第二类删掉，第三类写清宽许范围并指定谁来落实、何时落实
收尾时管住庆祝口径，公告里交代对方的去处和执行时间表
steps.en:
Sort every requirement into three piles: things you must get back, things useless to you but humiliating to them, and things that affect their livelihood
Cut the second pile; for the third, write down the scope of the indulgence and name who implements it and when
Keep the tone of celebration in check at the close, and in the announcement set out where the other side goes next and the execution timetable

alternative.zh: 作者提出的替代选择：也可反过来从严，把羞辱性条款当作威慑留下，好让对方记住谁说了算；代价是执行阶段缺少配合，而最容易卡住的往往是要对方经手的琐事。
alternative.en: The alternative the writer proposes: go the other way and keep the humiliating clauses as a show of force, so the other side remembers who gives the orders. The price is an absence of cooperation during execution, and the items most likely to stall are the small ones that only the other side's people can handle.

uncertainty_note.zh: 全文只有一个史源，即格兰特本人的回忆记述。对话是他的转述，未必逐字；他明言不知李的心情；本文不替任何一方补写心理；马匹宽许不在已写成的条文中，是格兰特当面答应李将指示留守军官办理的，其落实情况以及名册与宣誓的逐项执行，原文均未交代；日期按原文写法，不补年份。
uncertainty_note.en: There is only one source for this piece: Grant's own account in his memoirs. The conversations are his retellings and need not be verbatim; he says expressly that he did not know Lee's feelings, and this piece does not supply psychology for either side; the allowance on horses and mules was not in the written terms but promised to Lee as an instruction to the officers left behind, and neither its implementation nor the item-by-item execution of the rolls and paroles is reported; dates are kept in the original wording, with no year supplied.

preheader.zh: 格兰特提笔写受降条件时，不知道第一个词该写什么——但他中途加进了两样没人开口要的东西。
preheader.en: Grant sat down to write the surrender terms without knowing his first word — then added two things nobody had asked for.
